stem: A retail lender has historical applications with income, outstanding debt and a final label indicating whether the borrower defaulted. The lender wants to prioritize new applications for manual review by predicting a default category. The first release does not need to estimate the monetary loss. Which machine learning approach best matches this requirement?
options: Supervised classification using the historical default labels
Regression trained to estimate the outstanding loan balance
Unsupervised clustering followed by treating every cluster as a default class
Reinforcement learning using each new application as an action
reason: The required target is a known category, so labeled examples support supervised classification. Regression predicts a quantity; clusters do not automatically have default meanings; no reward-driven action loop is specified.
visual: Original application records → labeled training → new application → default-risk class; contrast category output with numeric loss.

stem: A subscription business wants to discover groups of customers with similar viewing and purchase behavior. It has usage records but has not defined customer segments or labeled examples. Analysts will inspect the resulting groups before designing campaigns. Which approach best fits the first stage?
options: Train a classifier on customer IDs as the desired segment labels
Use regression to predict the total number of customer segments
Apply reinforcement learning without defining actions or rewards
Apply clustering to discover patterns in the unlabeled behavior data
reason: Clustering discovers group structure without predefined targets. Customer IDs are identifiers rather than segment labels; regression and reward-based learning do not fit the stated discovery task.
visual: Customers as colored points → discovered groups → analyst interpretation; distinguish discovered clusters from pre-labeled categories.

stem: A warehouse simulator allows an automated cart to choose its next movement. The cart receives rewards for successful deliveries and penalties for collisions or excessive travel. The team wants it to improve its movement policy through repeated interaction with the simulator. Which learning approach is most appropriate?
options: Clustering delivery addresses without a reward signal
Regression that predicts package weight from dimensions
Reinforcement learning based on actions and resulting rewards
Supervised classification using only product category labels
reason: The task has an agent, environment, actions and reward feedback. The alternatives solve static prediction or grouping tasks rather than learning an action policy from interaction.
visual: Cart agent → movement action → simulated warehouse → reward/penalty → updated policy; use an original small warehouse layout.

stem: A support-ticket classifier achieves 99% accuracy on its training examples but only 72% on a separate, representative test set. The team has ruled out label-format errors. A stakeholder proposes reporting the training accuracy because it looks better. Which interpretation and next step are most appropriate?
options: Tune repeatedly against the test set and use the best observed test score as an unbiased estimate
Investigate overfitting and assess generalization using representative held-out data
Use the higher training score because the model has learned those examples successfully
Combine the training and test scores into one average and report that as generalization
reason: The gap suggests poor generalization and possible overfitting. Averaging away the gap or preferring the training score hides it; repeatedly tuning to the test set compromises its independence.
visual: Two scorecards: training 99%, held-out 72%; show generalization gap and evaluation loop, not an asserted universal fix.

stem: A bank screens transfers for fraud. Fraudulent transfers that pass undetected cause substantial losses, while investigators can tolerate reviewing additional alerts. The team wants a metric that directly measures the proportion of actual fraudulent transfers detected by the model. Which metric should it prioritize for this objective?
options: Recall for the fraud class
Precision for the fraud class
Overall accuracy without examining the minority class
Average model inference latency
reason: Recall measures detected fraud among all actual fraud. Precision measures the quality of alerts, while aggregate accuracy can hide missed rare cases. Latency is operational rather than detection quality.
visual: Confusion matrix with false negatives highlighted and recall = TP/(TP+FN); add business consequence of missed fraud.

stem: An insurance company uses a model to flag suspicious claims. Investigators report that most flagged claims are legitimate, consuming the available review capacity. The business wants to measure how often a flagged claim is actually suspicious before adjusting the decision threshold. Which metric is most directly relevant?
options: Recall calculated over all suspicious claims
The number of training epochs
Overall accuracy across a dataset dominated by legitimate claims
Precision for suspicious-claim predictions
reason: Precision describes true suspicious cases among flagged cases. Recall concerns missed suspicious cases, and overall accuracy may look high despite an inefficient alert queue. Threshold changes require evaluation of the precision–recall trade-off.
visual: Alert queue split into true and false positives; precision formula and review-capacity trade-off.

stem: A retailer plans to deploy a demand model in several regions. Its pilot evaluation uses mostly records from its largest urban store, although smaller stores have different seasonal patterns. The team wants a reliable estimate of deployment performance without leaking training data into evaluation. Which TWO actions are appropriate?
options: Evaluate on held-out examples representative of the deployment regions
Inspect performance separately for relevant store and seasonal groups
Add the held-out answers to training before calculating the reported test score
Keep only stores where the model already performs well
Use training accuracy as the sole estimate of deployment quality
reason: Representative held-out data and subgroup checks reveal generalization and local weaknesses. Test leakage, cherry-picking and training-only evaluation make the reported result less trustworthy.
visual: Training/test separation with region/store strata; show aggregate score alongside subgroup scores.

stem: A contact center stores recorded customer calls and wants searchable transcripts so supervisors can review conversations. The application does not need to generate speech or translate the calls into another language. The company prefers a managed AWS capability over operating its own speech-recognition model. Which service best meets this requirement?
options: Use Amazon Translate to turn the recorded audio directly into a same-language transcript
Use Amazon Transcribe to produce transcripts for authorized indexing and review
Use Amazon Polly to convert the stored calls into a searchable text transcript
Send the audio directly to Amazon Comprehend sentiment analysis and use its output as a verbatim transcript
reason: Transcribe converts supported audio speech into text. Polly creates audio from text, Translate changes language, and Comprehend analyzes existing text rather than directly transcribing audio.
visual: Stored call audio → Transcribe → timestamped transcript → authorized search/review; contrast audio/text input and output.

stem: A distributor receives scanned invoices from many suppliers. It needs to extract text, line items and supported form/table relationships before checking purchase-order totals. The solution should minimize custom document-model operations. Which approach is the best starting point?
options: Use Amazon Textract for supported document extraction and validate the business fields afterward
Use Amazon Comprehend entity detection alone to recover invoice table cells directly from scanned images
Use a text-only foundation model with invoice filenames as context to reconstruct missing line items
Use image label detection as the invoice parser and treat its object labels as validated accounting fields
reason: Textract supports extraction of document text and supported structure. Text analysis cannot directly recover scanned tables, an unseen filename is not invoice evidence, and visual object labels are not validated accounting fields. Validate extracted business values afterward.
visual: Invoice image → Textract → fields/tables → validation → exception review; label sample invoice as illustrative.

stem: A product team collects written customer reviews. It needs to identify sentiment and mentions of products in the existing text before preparing a service-quality dashboard. It does not need to generate new review text. Which managed AWS service is the most direct fit for these supported language-analysis tasks?
options: Use Amazon Translate to infer sentiment solely from translation confidence
Use Amazon Personalize to interpret every review as a recommendation ranking and return entity spans
Use Amazon Lex intent configuration as a direct replacement for batch sentiment and entity analysis
Use Amazon Comprehend for supported sentiment and entity analysis of the existing text
reason: Comprehend directly supports the requested language analysis. Translation confidence is not sentiment, recommendation ranking is not entity-span detection, and configured conversational intents are not a substitute for the specified analysis of existing review text.
visual: Review text → sentiment/entity analysis → aggregated dashboard; show confidence as prediction, not certainty about customer intent.

stem: A manufacturer scores one million stored component records each night. The results are needed for a morning planning report, and no user waits for an immediate prediction. The team wants to avoid maintaining an always-on inference endpoint solely for this workload. Which inference pattern is most suitable?
options: Score every record interactively during report viewing, even though the full report is required at opening
Use a conversational agent to decide which records to skip without an agreed completeness criterion
Run an offline batch inference job against the stored inputs and collect the results for the report
Keep a real-time endpoint running continuously because stored inputs require synchronous predictions
reason: Batch inference fits stored data with a later reporting deadline. Continuous real-time capacity is not required for that pattern, interactive report-time scoring conflicts with the ready-at-opening requirement, and arbitrary record skipping violates completeness.
visual: S3 input dataset → batch inference job → S3 predictions → morning report; contrast latency requirements with interactive inference.

topic: When AI is not the appropriate tool
stem: A finance team must apply a published tax rule with fixed thresholds and exact rounding. The rules change through an approved policy process, and the same valid inputs must always produce the same statutory result. There is no need to infer an unknown value from historical examples. What should the team choose first?
options: Train a classifier on historical tax brackets and let it infer the required rounding rules
Implement the specified calculation as deterministic rules with validation and controlled updates
Use a language model to reproduce the published rule and accept any plausible formatted result
Train a regression model on last year’s outputs and use its prediction as the exact statutory result
reason: Exact, specified calculations suit deterministic logic. Predictive or generative approaches introduce avoidable uncertainty when the required rule is already known.
visual: Known rule + inputs → deterministic calculation → exact result; contrast prediction with rule execution.

stem: A delivery-time model is live and initially met its approved quality criteria. Place the following lifecycle activities in a logical order when evaluating a controlled improvement after a business change. Use each response once.
options: Release the approved candidate through the controlled deployment process
Monitor production data and prediction quality
Investigate the observed change and prepare a candidate update
Evaluate the candidate against representative held-out and business acceptance criteria
reason: Production monitoring identifies the change, investigation informs an update, evaluation establishes whether the candidate meets requirements, and a controlled release follows approval. A change does not justify blindly replacing the model.
visual: Launch → monitor data/quality → investigate route change → evaluate candidate → approved release; distinguish system health from model quality.

stem: A retailer wants to create draft product descriptions from approved product facts. It also has a separate need to predict whether a shipment will arrive late. The team must explain the difference to stakeholders before selecting services. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two tasks?
options: Both are classification tasks because each starts from existing business data
Both are generative tasks because every predicted label is newly produced text
The distinction depends only on whether the application uses a managed endpoint
Description drafting generates new content; late-arrival classification predicts a defined category
reason: Generating text and predicting a category are distinct capabilities. Historical data alone does not make a task generative, and custom foundation-model pre-training is not a prerequisite.
visual: Two lanes: approved facts → generated description; shipment features → late/on-time class.

stem: A travel company is evaluating foundation models for a multilingual support assistant. The service must meet response-time and quality requirements in several customer languages while staying within a defined budget. Which TWO evaluation practices best support selecting a suitable model?
options: Use representative examples in the required languages and measure answer quality
Measure latency and applicable input/output costs on the expected workload
Select the largest parameter count without testing the required languages
Compare only the advertised input-token price and ignore generated output usage
Use one successful English example as evidence of quality in every language
reason: Representative multilingual quality tests and workload measurements support the stated requirements. Size, one pricing unit and a single-language example do not establish suitability.
visual: Model comparison matrix with language quality, latency, cost and acceptance thresholds; no invented live vendor prices.

stem: An assistant produces fluent answers about products, but a reviewer finds specifications that do not exist in the approved catalog. Management proposes removing citations so users will focus on the prose. Which response best addresses the underlying issue?
options: Reduce temperature and consider factual verification unnecessary once answers become more consistent
Ground answers in approved catalog evidence, evaluate factual support and define behavior for evidence gaps
Fine-tune on a one-time catalog snapshot and assume future generated specifications will stay current
Require citations in the output format but allow the model to invent the cited source details
reason: Evidence grounding and evaluation address unsupported claims. Fine-tuning a snapshot does not keep facts current, citation formatting can still be fabricated, and low randomness does not guarantee accuracy.
visual: Catalog evidence → retrieval → grounded answer; unsupported specification branch → acknowledge uncertainty/escalate.
caseContext: Case study: A retailer is piloting an assistant that answers employee questions from an approved internal product catalog. The catalog changes frequently. Some product groups are restricted to particular teams. Pilot answers are fluent, but reviewers have found unsupported specifications.

stem: A small company wants to compare several supported foundation models through managed APIs. It has no team to operate GPU-based model-serving infrastructure and needs to begin with text-generation experiments. Which AWS service is the most suitable starting point?
options: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker AI with fully customer-managed model hosting as the only option
Amazon EC2 GPU instances with a self-installed inference server
AWS Artifact used as a model inference endpoint
reason: Bedrock offers managed access to supported foundation models. Self-managed hosting may fit other needs but adds the operational work excluded by this scenario; Artifact supplies compliance documents.
visual: Application → Bedrock API → supported model choices; operational responsibility comparison with self-hosting.

stem: A knowledge-search team wants queries about an employee leaving the company to retrieve relevant offboarding documents even when the documents use different words. The search must consider meaning rather than depend only on exact keyword matches. Which concept is most relevant?
options: Use exact keyword matching alone and assume synonyms will always match without configuration
Rank all documents by sentiment score and treat similar sentiment as similar subject matter
Compare vectors from independently chosen incompatible embedding models because both outputs are numeric
Use compatible document/query embeddings and evaluate semantic retrieval on representative queries
reason: Compatible embeddings support semantic retrieval across different wording. Exact keyword matching alone does not guarantee synonym handling, sentiment is not general subject similarity, and numeric vectors from incompatible models are not automatically comparable.
visual: Query wording and differently phrased document → compatible vectors → nearby semantic matches; not a claim of perfect retrieval.

stem: A legal team submits a very long document together with instructions and asks for a detailed summary. The selected model rejects the request because it exceeds its supported context capacity. Which approach most directly addresses the limitation?
options: Increase the permitted output length without reducing input or checking the total model limit
Assume all stored documents are available to the model even when they are not included or retrieved
Select relevant content or a suitable larger-context model while budgeting input and output tokens
Increase the connection timeout and resubmit the same oversized request unchanged
reason: The model context limit is separate from network timeouts and storage. Select relevant content or suitable supported capacity and budget both input and output; a longer timeout or uploaded document alone does not change what the model can process.
visual: Context-budget bar: instructions + document excerpts + reserved output; distinguish upload storage from model context.

stem: A support assistant takes several seconds to finish a long answer. Users would benefit from seeing useful text earlier, and the chosen model/API supports streamed responses. The business does not require the entire response to be available before displaying any text. Which change best addresses the user experience?
options: Increase the requested answer length and assume that guarantees a shorter time to first output
Render supported streamed response events progressively, with partial-output and failure handling
Use a streaming API but buffer all events until the final answer is complete
Cache the completed answer only and assume every first-time question will have a cache hit
reason: Displaying supported stream events can improve time to visible output. Buffering until the final event loses that benefit. Caching does not guarantee hits for new questions, and requesting more output does not guarantee a faster first token.
visual: Time-to-first-output versus total completion timeline; streamed chunks with error/cancel handling.

stem: A team compares two text models. Model A has a lower input-token price but produces much longer answers on the representative workload. Model B has a higher input price and shorter useful responses. What should the team do before concluding which option costs less?
options: Measure representative input/output usage and apply each model’s current applicable pricing
Compare input-token prices alone and omit output charges from both estimates
Compare character counts while assuming identical tokenization across models
Compare maximum context sizes and assume the smallest limit guarantees the lowest workload cost
reason: Total inference cost depends on applicable usage and pricing dimensions, including output usage where charged. Tokenization and deployment choices can differ.
visual: Two workload cost ledgers: input units + output units + applicable options; use illustrative prices only.

stem: A company uses an existing foundation model to draft a reply from instructions and a customer message. It does not run a training job or update model weights. Which statement accurately describes this operation?
options: It is fine-tuning because the model changes its response based on request context
It is pre-training because the message is new information to the application
It is continuous pre-training because several messages are sent in one conversation
It is inference using an existing model without an ordinary prompt updating its weights
reason: A model can use request context during inference without weight updates. Prompting is not itself pre-training or fine-tuning, and inputs are not automatically labeled training examples.
visual: Pre-training/adaptation timeline separated from inference request → response; mark weights unchanged by ordinary prompting.

stem: A software team wants AI assistance that can turn feature requirements into structured specifications and help implement changes in its development workflow. The team will continue reviewing and testing generated code. Which AWS offering is the most relevant to evaluate?
options: Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases alone as a complete specification-to-code development environment
Use SageMaker model training jobs as a direct substitute for code review and application development
Evaluate Kiro for AI-assisted specification and development workflows
Use Amazon Quick Sight dashboard authoring as the primary source-code implementation workflow
reason: Kiro is relevant to AI-assisted development and specification workflows. Dashboard authoring, knowledge retrieval alone and model training jobs do not provide the stated specification-to-application development assistance. Generated changes still require review and testing.
visual: Requirements → specification → proposed implementation → tests/review, with Kiro as an assistant rather than an approval authority.

stem: An operations team wants a workplace AI experience that can bring together authorized company information, business insights and supported actions. It is evaluating current offerings for a new deployment rather than onboarding a new legacy Q Business application. Which AWS offering is the best fit to assess?
options: Use Amazon Lex intent configuration alone and assume all enterprise data, BI and actions are already integrated
Evaluate Amazon Quick’s supported workplace AI, insights and action capabilities
Use Amazon Comprehend alone as the end-to-end workplace research and action experience
Use an S3 bucket plus keyword filenames and assume it supplies an authorized conversational workplace assistant
reason: Amazon Quick addresses supported workplace AI and insights/actions use cases. Text analysis alone, object storage alone, or an intent configuration alone does not automatically supply the complete authorized enterprise experience described.
visual: Authorized enterprise sources → Quick capabilities → insights/actions; preserve separate data permissions and action authorization.

stem: A media company is assessing model capabilities for three different business tasks. Match each task to the most appropriate capability to evaluate. Use each response once.
options: Compatible text embeddings
Image generation
Image-and-text understanding
reason: Content creation, multimodal understanding and semantic representation are different capabilities. Support for one does not guarantee suitability for the other tasks; each needs representative evaluation.
visual: Three original capability lanes: written brief → image generation; photo plus incident text → multimodal understanding; document/query text → compatible embeddings and semantic comparison.
prompts: Create new promotional images from written briefs
Interpret a component photograph together with an incident report
Compare differently worded document passages by semantic similarity

stem: A startup compares a managed model API with hosting an open-weight model on its own compute. The self-hosted estimate includes only accelerator rental, while the managed estimate includes all per-request charges. Which additional factors are necessary for a fair comparison?
options: Compare accelerator rental with managed input-token charges and exclude all other dimensions
Assume self-hosting is always cheaper because there is no managed per-request invoice
Assume managed inference is always cheaper regardless of throughput, utilization and requirements
Include utilization, scaling, availability, security and operational effort in the comparison
reason: Infrastructure cost alone omits engineering and operational responsibilities. Utilization and service requirements can materially change the total cost of a self-hosted option.
visual: Managed API versus self-hosted responsibility/cost stack; include operations and utilization, not live dollar claims.

stem: A marketing company wants generative AI to accelerate first drafts while preserving factual accuracy and brand requirements. Which TWO practices best support this objective?
options: Have reviewers validate factual claims and brand-sensitive content before publication
Evaluate representative prompts and outputs against documented quality criteria
Treat every grammatical response as verified factual content
Remove the approval workflow because the model was pre-trained on large datasets
Assume a single successful example proves reliability for every campaign
reason: Human validation and representative evaluation support controlled use. Grammar, training scale and isolated success do not establish factual reliability across the workload.
visual: AI first draft → factual/brand checks → approved publication, with a separate representative evaluation loop.

stem: A team has selected an agent-development framework and now needs to evaluate managed capabilities for running and operating agents. It wants to avoid assuming the framework alone provides all production runtime and identity facilities. Which AWS offering should it assess for these managed agent capabilities?
options: Treat a prompt template as a replacement for runtime, identity and operational capabilities
Evaluate Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for supported managed agent operational capabilities
Assume installing an agent framework also provides a managed runtime and workload identity by default
Use a vector store alone as the complete agent hosting and operational platform
reason: AgentCore provides managed agent-related capabilities; an orchestration framework and an operational platform have different roles. The other services do not provide that overall agent capability set.
visual: Agent framework/application above managed runtime, identity and operational capabilities; avoid claiming every feature is automatic.

topic: Traditional ML versus a foundation model
stem: A utility has millions of structured meter records and needs to predict a numeric demand value for planning. It does not need conversational text or content generation. Before committing to a foundation model, what is the most appropriate approach?
options: Compare suitable traditional predictive models against accuracy, explainability and cost requirements
Choose a language model solely because its text responses are more fluent
Require foundation-model pre-training before testing any structured-data baseline
Convert every numeric record into prose and assume the conversion guarantees better demand prediction
reason: Structured numeric prediction can suit traditional ML. The choice should follow measured requirements rather than treating generative AI as mandatory.
visual: Structured meter data → candidate regression/forecasting approaches → quality/cost/business comparison; no implementation-heavy tuning detail.

stem: For the retailer in case study CATALOG-01, employees need answers from a catalog that changes weekly. Answers must identify supporting catalog passages and respect restrictions on product groups. The team wants to avoid model training after each catalog edit. Which approach best fits these requirements?
options: Fine-tune on every catalog revision and assume model memory enforces each employee’s document permissions
Use a static prompt containing a single old catalog snapshot and assume weekly updates appear automatically
Increase output length and ask the model to supply citations even when no source evidence is retrieved
Use RAG with updated authorized sources and evaluate citation support
reason: RAG can supply updated catalog evidence at inference time with the required permission checks. Fine-tuned model memory does not enforce per-employee document access, a static snapshot does not acquire weekly edits, and citation formatting without evidence can be fabricated.
visual: Catalog update/ingestion -> authorized retrieval by employee group -> model context -> cited answer; show the permission gate before generation.
caseContext: Case study: A retailer is piloting an assistant that answers employee questions from an approved internal product catalog. The catalog changes frequently. Some product groups are restricted to particular teams. Pilot answers are fluent, but reviewers have found unsupported specifications.

stem: A company has already ingested and indexed its approved support documentation. A customer now asks a product question. Place the following application steps in the logical order for a grounded RAG answer. Use every response once.
options: Generate a response using the supplied evidence
Receive the customer’s question
Retrieve relevant authorized passages
Construct the model request using the question and retrieved passages
reason: After receiving the question, the application retrieves relevant authorized evidence, constructs the request context, and generates the response. Document ingestion is a separate earlier activity.
visual: Numbered request-time RAG architecture, with the indexing path shown separately as already completed.

stem: A company already supplies up-to-date product facts through retrieval. Its remaining problem is that responses do not consistently follow a specialized writing style, despite prompt experimentation. It has a large curated set of approved input-output examples and an eligible model. Which approach should it evaluate for behavior adaptation?
options: Use the training examples as the only evaluation set and treat memorization as successful generalization
Evaluate fine-tuning on representative approved examples while retaining retrieval and independent testing
Add more unrelated documents to the vector index and assume that teaches the target writing style
Replace retrieved current facts with model memory so answers have fewer source constraints
reason: Fine-tuning may adapt behavior or style when eligible models and suitable examples exist. More unrelated retrieval content does not teach the requested style; dropping current evidence harms grounding, and training examples alone cannot independently establish generalization.
visual: Keep knowledge retrieval lane; separate curated examples → eligible fine-tuning → behavior evaluation → style-adapted model.

stem: A logistics company wants delivery exceptions summarized in a consistent three-field format. The team prefers to try a request-level approach before changing model weights. Which prompt strategy is the best next experiment?
options: Add clear instructions and several representative demonstrations of the required output
Provide only the field names and let the model choose what each field should mean
Increase sampling randomness so that more responses happen to match the required format
Repeat ordinary requests and assume the model’s weights are permanently updated without a training process
reason: Few-shot examples demonstrate the requested behavior in context. Ordinary prompting does not itself update weights, and stronger variability does not enforce a schema. Validation remains necessary.
visual: Task instruction + worked examples + new exception → structured draft → schema/business validation.

stem: A claims assistant receives the instruction “review this” followed by a long report. Results vary between a summary, a coverage decision and a list of missing documents. The business only wants a factual summary and does not authorize automated coverage decisions. Which prompt change is most appropriate?
options: Keep the ambiguous instruction and ask the model to choose the most useful business action
Increase maximum output length so the model can include every possible interpretation of the task
Remove the report context and ask for a generic claim response from model memory
State the summary-only task, relevant context, output structure and the boundary against coverage decisions
reason: Explicit task and output boundaries reduce ambiguity. They guide model behavior but do not replace trusted authorization for consequential actions. More output capacity does not resolve an unspecified task.
visual: Ambiguous prompt branching into three outputs versus explicit summary-only contract; put action authorization outside the model.

stem: A team extracts a small set of facts with a supported text model. It wants more consistent and usable responses but cannot assume every generated value is correct. Which TWO actions are appropriate?
options: Evaluate supported lower-randomness settings and appropriate output limits
Validate output structure and relevant business facts before accepting the result
Treat lower randomness as a guarantee that every extracted value is true
Skip validation whenever the output is valid JSON
Apply identical parameter ranges to all models without checking support
reason: Sampling and output controls can improve consistency, while validation checks usability and correctness. Lower randomness or valid JSON alone does not guarantee factual accuracy.
visual: Parameter controls → output consistency/length experiments → validation; separate permissions from inference behavior.

stem: A search application replaces its query embedding model but continues searching document vectors created by a different model. The new model uses a different vector representation, and retrieval quality drops. What is the most appropriate corrective approach?
options: Increase answer-model context length while leaving the incompatible retrieval configuration unchanged
Coordinate compatible document/query embeddings and rebuild affected vectors as needed
Keep the incompatible vectors and assume equal numeric dimensions guarantee semantic compatibility
Normalize vector magnitude alone and assume that aligns independently learned embedding spaces
reason: Document and query representations must be compatible. Matching vector dimensions or magnitudes alone does not align independently learned semantic spaces. Rebuild affected vectors and validate retrieval rather than only changing the downstream answer context limit.
visual: Old embedding space versus new space → coordinated re-embedding → validated document/query retrieval.

stem: A policy assistant often retrieves a section heading but not the paragraph containing its exception. The answer model then provides an incomplete policy summary. The team has verified that the source document contains the missing paragraph. Which area should it investigate first?
options: Investigate extraction, chunking and retrieval quality using representative exception questions
Increase only output length, even when the needed exception never reaches model context
Fine-tune the generator on response style without inspecting missing retrieval evidence
Reduce sampling randomness and assume the model can recover any omitted source paragraph
reason: The missing exception is an evidence-pipeline problem to investigate through extraction, chunking and retrieval tests. More output capacity, style adaptation or lower randomness cannot reliably supply an omitted source paragraph.
visual: Document section/exception → chunk boundaries → retrieval results → supported answer; highlight missing evidence.

stem: A customer assistant can look up orders and request cancellations through tools. A customer asks to cancel an order that belongs to another account. The model produces a well-formed cancellation request. What control is essential before executing the action?
options: Execute any syntactically valid tool request because JSON validity demonstrates permission
Depend only on a prompt telling the agent to cancel orders for the correct customer
Cancel first and check ownership afterward using the resulting audit record
Enforce customer ownership and cancellation authorization in trusted execution code before the action
reason: Syntactic validity is not authorization. Trusted execution code must enforce ownership, permissions and any required approval before a consequential operation.
visual: User → agent-proposed action → trusted ownership/permission gate → cancellation API; denied branch before side effect.

stem: An invoice application always extracts fields, checks required values, and sends exceptions to a reviewer. The stages and routing conditions are known in advance. A stakeholder asks to add unrestricted agent planning even though no new decision flexibility is required. Which design choice is most appropriate?
options: Replace the validation stage with an agent’s verbal assurance that fields look correct
Grant the agent broad finance access so it can invent new processing steps without review
Use an explicit workflow and add autonomy only for requirements that need it
Let an agent select and reorder all stages even though the approved sequence is already known
reason: Known stages and branches fit an explicit workflow. Unnecessary autonomy and broad permissions increase uncertainty without meeting a stated need; validation remains an application responsibility.
visual: Defined extraction → validation → approved path/exception branch; contrast controlled flow with unnecessary open-ended planning.

stem: A team sends a large unchanged instruction prefix on many requests to a model that supports prompt caching. It wants to reduce repeated processing cost without changing the task or its evaluation criteria. Which option should it evaluate?
options: Fine-tune once and assume the application no longer needs to supply any request-specific context
Evaluate eligible prompt caching under the selected model’s support and charging rules
Store conversation transcripts and assume this automatically enables provider-side prompt caching
Increase response randomness to avoid the cost of repeatedly interpreting the same instructions
reason: Prompt caching can reuse eligible repeated prompt content. Support and charging rules vary; persistent conversation storage and sampling settings are not the same capability.
visual: Repeated eligible prefix → cache reuse/miss paths → usage/cost comparison; label model-specific support and retention.

stem: A company has a larger model that performs well on a specialized task. It wants to explore a smaller model that reproduces useful task behavior with potentially lower serving cost, subject to an acceptable quality trade-off. Which technique is most directly relevant?
options: Evaluate model distillation from the teacher to the smaller student, with quality testing
Use RAG alone and describe document retrieval as a transfer of the teacher’s weights
Increase the student’s context window and assume it automatically inherits teacher behavior
Change output formatting and assume the smaller model now has identical teacher capabilities
reason: Distillation transfers useful behavior from a teacher to a student model. It requires quality evaluation; a smaller model is not guaranteed to preserve every capability.
visual: Teacher guidance → curated transfer examples/training → student model → quality/latency/cost evaluation.

stem: A team updates a production prompt and later needs to investigate why answer behavior changed. Several developers edited the same untracked text file, and the deployed model settings were not recorded. Which practice best supports reproducibility and rollback?
options: Keep only response timestamps and assume they identify the exact deployed instructions
Overwrite one shared prompt file and rely on team memory for rollback
Retain only the latest successful answer as a reproducible record of the entire release
Version prompts and record model/configuration details for each controlled release
reason: Versioned prompts and configuration records support investigation and controlled rollback. Timestamps alone do not identify the instructions and settings that produced an answer.
visual: Mutable draft → reviewed version → deployment record → monitored release/rollback; include model/configuration alongside prompt version.

stem: A team uses a second language model to score the helpfulness of generated answers. It wants to scale evaluation but has not checked whether the judge’s ratings agree with knowledgeable human reviewers. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Keep only high-scoring examples in the evaluation set to obtain a stable positive rating
Choose the judge with the most parameters without measuring agreement with the quality criteria
Calibrate judge ratings against representative human assessments and investigate systematic bias
Assume using a different model makes the judge automatically objective
reason: Model-based evaluation needs validation and calibration. A different model can still have biases, and selective evaluation does not establish broad quality.
visual: Generated answers → human reference judgments + model judge → agreement/bias checks → calibrated evaluation process.

stem: A travel assistant scores well on a text-similarity benchmark, but users still abandon sessions because answers arrive too slowly and fail to complete itinerary tasks. Which TWO additional measures best address the product team’s concern?
options: User-perceived latency and satisfaction
Only the number of model parameters
Only the number of words in the system prompt
Only the training duration of the base model
Task completion rate on representative user journeys
reason: Application success includes user outcomes and operational experience as well as model-level benchmarks. Parameter counts, prompt length and training duration do not directly measure completed travel tasks.
visual: Model benchmark plus user journey → completion, latency, satisfaction and cost dashboard.

stem: An assistant retrieves a document containing relevant troubleshooting instructions. The document also includes text telling the assistant to ignore its rules and send an internal credential to an external destination. The content came from an indexed source, but it is not a trusted instruction channel. Which response best addresses the risk?
options: Treat retrieved content as untrusted and enforce secret/tool access boundaries outside the model
Execute retrieved instructions whenever the document has a high similarity score
Assume quotation marks around retrieved text guarantee universal injection protection
Allow the model to decide whether to disclose credentials based only on its self-reported confidence
reason: Retrieved content must not gain instruction authority merely by being relevant. Layered prompt defenses and trusted data/tool controls are needed; delimiters alone are not a security guarantee.
visual: Untrusted retrieval → instruction/data boundary → least-privilege tools and secret controls; blocked exfiltration path.

stem: A company tests an assistant with a configured content guardrail. Some prohibited outputs are blocked, but the team has tested only a small set of English prompts and the application also serves other languages. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Treat successful blocking of a few prompts as proof of safety for all languages and future inputs
Use content filtering as a substitute for checking each user’s access to source documents
Stop monitoring once the guardrail has been enabled for the production endpoint
Continue representative safety testing with layered controls, monitoring and appropriate authorization
reason: A guardrail is one risk-reduction control with a defined scope. Representative testing, monitoring and authorization remain necessary; a few successful tests do not prove universal safety.
visual: Layered safety controls with multilingual evaluation → monitoring → incident review; keep IAM/data permissions separate.

stem: A company prepares examples to adapt an eligible foundation model for customer-service responses. The collected data includes outdated answers, duplicate conversations and sensitive customer identifiers. Which TWO actions should occur before training?
options: Curate accurate, representative examples and separate evaluation data
Review permissions and sensitive data handling for the intended training use
Include all historical answers regardless of correctness to maximize dataset size
Use production customer identifiers whenever the model asks for more context
Evaluate only on exact duplicates of the training conversations
reason: Data quality, representativeness, governance and independent evaluation matter. More low-quality or improperly governed data can introduce errors and privacy risk; duplicates undermine evaluation.
visual: Raw examples → quality/rights/privacy gates → curated training + held-out evaluation → eligible adaptation.

stem: A hiring-support model has strong overall accuracy, but an audit finds substantially more qualified candidates from one group are incorrectly rejected. The team has permission to conduct the relevant fairness assessment. Which action best addresses the finding?
options: Change the reporting threshold solely to hide the gap without evaluating business impact
Evaluate subgroup errors and investigate data, labels and process causes
Use aggregate accuracy alone because all subgroup errors are included in the average
Exclude the affected group from reporting without addressing the observed failures
reason: Aggregate performance can conceal unequal error patterns. Investigate representativeness, labels and the decision process. Excluding a group or adjusting reporting solely to hide the gap does not address the observed harm.
visual: Aggregate score split into subgroup confusion matrices → cause investigation → mitigation/re-evaluation; avoid equating correlation with causation.

stem: A loan-support tool identifies income and outstanding debt as influential inputs for a particular risk prediction. A stakeholder interprets the explanation as proof that changing either value will cause a specific approval outcome. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Explain that feature influence does not by itself establish causality or a guaranteed decision outcome
Treat a high attribution value as proof that changing the feature causes approval
Treat explainability as proof that the model has no unfair subgroup outcomes
Replace outcome validation with attribution plots because explanations make testing unnecessary
reason: Attributions can help explain predictions but do not automatically establish causality, fairness or future outcomes. Those require separate evidence and governance.
visual: Prediction with signed feature contributions → influence explanation; separate blocked inference arrow from attribution to proven causation.

stem: A healthcare organization uses AI to highlight potentially important information in clinical notes. It wants the system to support qualified clinicians rather than independently determine treatment. Which design is most consistent with this objective?
options: Treat a condition mention extracted from text as a confirmed clinical diagnosis
Allow treatment decisions automatically whenever the language model expresses high confidence
Use the AI’s written recommendation as the only evidence required by the clinician
Present evidence and limitations and preserve meaningful clinician review of significant decisions
reason: Decision support needs appropriate evidence, limitations and meaningful oversight. Entity extraction and fluent text do not establish a diagnosis or authorize treatment.
visual: Clinical text → extraction/assistance → evidence and uncertainty → clinician review → decision; clearly label AI output as support.

stem: An organization shares a model with several internal business units. Users need to know the intended use, evaluation results, important limitations and situations where the model should not be relied on. Which deliverable best supports this need?
options: Publish only a technical model identifier without use limitations or evaluation context
Record only the latest aggregate score and omit the population and conditions evaluated
Maintain model documentation covering intended use, evaluation, limitations and review responsibilities
Provide only average infrastructure uptime as the model’s transparency record
reason: Maintained model documentation communicates purpose, evaluation context, limitations and review responsibilities. Infrastructure uptime, an identifier alone or an unqualified aggregate score does not provide that transparency.
visual: Original model-card layout: purpose, data/evaluation summary, limitations, oversight and review date.

stem: An image classifier performs well on clear catalog photographs but often fails on representative warehouse images with poor lighting and partial obstruction. The business expects those conditions in normal operation. Which quality should the team investigate most directly?
options: Assume high overall accuracy on a different image population guarantees warehouse performance
Assess robustness using representative variations in lighting and obstruction
Evaluate only clear catalog images because they produced the best original score
Raise the displayed confidence label without changing evaluation or model behavior
reason: Robustness should be assessed under representative operating conditions. Restricting tests to favorable images or changing a displayed confidence label does not fix the weakness; results on another population do not establish warehouse performance.
visual: Clear versus low-light/occluded inputs → performance comparison → representative robustness test matrix.

stem: A company wants to publish AI-generated customer advice. Pilot testing finds occasionally harmful or misleading responses, and the business serves users with varied needs. Which TWO practices best support responsible deployment?
options: Discard complaints so they do not affect the model’s aggregate score
Use only the most successful prompt as the entire safety test set
Test representative harmful/misleading cases and define acceptable-use boundaries
Provide proportionate human escalation, monitoring and incident response
Assume a content filter removes every need for ongoing oversight
reason: Representative risk testing and an operational response process support responsible use. Filters and a favorable example do not eliminate the need for continued evaluation or user recourse.
visual: Risk assessment → representative tests → layered controls → human escalation/incident learning.

stem: A team can access a collection of third-party reports and wants to use them to train a commercial model. The project owner assumes access permission automatically grants all training and redistribution rights. What should the team do before using the reports?
options: Assume authenticated access grants every possible training and redistribution right
Remove attribution and assume that automatically authorizes reuse
Encrypt the dataset and treat storage confidentiality as a complete usage-rights assessment
Review provenance, applicable permissions and intended reuse with responsible owners
reason: The ability to access material is different from permission for every reuse. Provenance and applicable terms require review; anonymizing attribution or encrypting storage does not settle those rights.
visual: Access permission versus reuse rights as separate gates → documented permitted use; avoid asserting a universal legal outcome.

stem: A regulated business compares two models. One has slightly better predictive performance, while the other offers explanations that stakeholders can evaluate more effectively. The business has documented requirements for both decision quality and understandable review. What is the most appropriate selection process?
options: Choose the more interpretable model without checking its minimum decision-quality performance
Treat understandable explanations as proof of both accuracy and absence of bias
Compare both models against documented performance, explainability and risk requirements
Choose the highest aggregate predictive score regardless of the review requirements
reason: Model selection should reflect the stated requirements and trade-offs. Neither a higher score nor simpler explanations alone establish overall suitability.
visual: Quality/explainability/risk decision matrix with required thresholds; show a trade-off rather than an automatic winner.

stem: A customer assistant passed its launch review, but users later report that its advice is misleading after a business policy change. The team can reproduce the problem. Which response best follows responsible AI practice?
options: Respond only if infrastructure availability declines, regardless of misleading advice
Investigate impact, constrain or correct affected behavior, and re-evaluate before restoring reliance
Continue unchanged because launch approval is sufficient for all later policy conditions
Remove the failing examples from quality reports while keeping the production behavior
reason: Responsible operation continues after launch. Reproducible harmful or misleading behavior needs investigation and proportionate response even when infrastructure is healthy.
visual: User report → impact triage → containment/correction → re-evaluation → monitored release.

stem: An AI application needs to read approved documents from one S3 prefix. It must not modify the documents or access unrelated business files. The workload runs on an AWS service that supports IAM roles. Which access approach is most appropriate?
options: Use a workload role with required read actions limited to the approved S3 resource scope
Use a workload role with account-wide S3 read/write access to reduce future permission changes
Use a shared long-lived access key with broad read permissions in every processing job
Grant access to the approved bucket but allow unnecessary write and delete operations
reason: A scoped role supports least-privilege workload access. Broad policies and embedded long-lived credentials add unnecessary exposure and do not match the stated need.
visual: Application role → narrowly scoped S3 read permission → approved prefix; blocked write/unrelated-prefix requests.

topic: Audit activity versus model content logging
stem: A security team needs a record of supported AWS API activity associated with an AI application, including who called an operation and when. It also recognizes that recording full model prompts and responses is a separate logging decision. Which service is most directly relevant to the API audit requirement?
options: Use only aggregate CloudWatch performance metrics as an identity-level API activity trail
Use model prompt/response logs alone and assume they record every relevant AWS API operation
Use AWS Artifact reports as a live record of the application’s API calls
Use AWS CloudTrail with supported audit-event collection configured for the needed operations
reason: CloudTrail supports API activity auditing with appropriate event collection. Aggregate performance metrics are not an identity-level activity trail, prompt/response content logs do not replace API auditing, and Artifact reports are not a live activity stream.
visual: Caller/API request → CloudTrail event metadata; separate model invocation-content logging lane with privacy/access controls.

stem: A company plans to use documents stored in S3 for an AI knowledge source. Before onboarding the data, it wants to identify potentially sensitive information so the data owners can assess and remediate exposure. Which AWS service best fits the discovery requirement?
options: Use CloudTrail access-event records as a complete classification of the documents’ contents
Use S3 object sizes and filenames alone as a sufficient sensitive-data assessment
Use Amazon Macie discovery findings to support data-owner assessment of the S3 content
Use KMS encryption status as proof that the objects contain no sensitive information
reason: Macie discovery findings support sensitive-data assessment in S3. Encryption status does not show content is non-sensitive, API activity logs do not fully classify document contents, and sizes or filenames alone are insufficient.
visual: S3 inventory → Macie discovery findings → data-owner assessment → remediation/approved AI ingestion.

stem: An AI project needs three complementary capabilities: an audit record of supported AWS API activity, discovery of sensitive information in S3, and management of encryption keys. Match each requirement to the most appropriate AWS service. Use each response once.
options: AWS KMS
Amazon Macie
AWS CloudTrail
reason: CloudTrail addresses API activity auditing, Macie sensitive-data discovery in S3, and KMS cryptographic key management. None replaces the application’s authorization controls.
visual: Three independent security lanes with input, service and output; emphasize complementary roles.

topic: Encryption at rest and in transit
stem: A company encrypts the documents stored for its AI application but discovers that one application connection does not use appropriate transport protection. The owner argues that storage encryption already protects every stage. Which TWO statements are correct?
options: Encryption at rest guarantees that all network traffic is encrypted
A larger foundation model automatically supplies transport encryption
IAM authorization eliminates the need to consider network confidentiality
Storage encryption and encryption in transit protect different parts of the data lifecycle
Appropriate transport protection such as TLS should be assessed for the application connection
reason: At-rest and in-transit protection address different exposure points. Transport security needs its own configuration and validation; model size and access permission are not substitutes.
visual: Stored encrypted object → application transport path → model/service connection; label at-rest and TLS boundaries separately.

stem: An application team has placed a shared long-lived AWS access key in configuration used by several AI processing jobs. The jobs run in an environment that supports IAM roles and temporary credentials. Which change best reduces credential exposure while retaining necessary access?
options: Store the existing shared long-lived key in an approved secret store but leave all jobs using the same broad identity
Issue a different administrator key to every job without reducing permissions
Copy the same key into every job image so credential retrieval is simpler
Use scoped workload roles and temporary credentials supported by the job environment
reason: Supported workload roles and scoped temporary credentials reduce reliance on shared long-lived keys. A secret store may improve storage of an existing key but retains the shared identity, while administrator keys and copied image secrets add exposure without least privilege.
visual: Workload → role credentials → authorized API; contrast temporary scoped identity with copied shared keys.

stem: A company wants a private application to access a supported managed AI service without routing that application traffic over the public internet. An architect proposes evaluating the service’s VPC endpoint options. Which statement correctly describes the design consideration?
options: Treat endpoint reachability as proof that every caller is authorized to invoke the model
Assume the endpoint alone replaces all applicable DNS, identity and endpoint-policy configuration
Use supported endpoints for private connectivity while retaining the AWS-managed service boundary
Treat endpoint creation as moving the service’s underlying runtime into the customer subnet
reason: Private connectivity and service ownership boundaries are distinct. Network paths still need appropriate DNS and authorization controls; an endpoint is not a universal permission grant.
visual: Private application subnet → supported endpoint/PrivateLink → AWS-managed service boundary; separate network and IAM gates.

stem: An enterprise is assessing an AI workload and needs relevant AWS compliance reports for its vendor assessment. It must also evaluate its own application configuration and operational controls. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Assume managed hosting removes the need for evidence about customer data and identity controls
Obtain relevant AWS reports through Artifact and separately assess customer application responsibilities
Treat the provider’s compliance report as automatic certification of every customer configuration
Use API audit logs alone as a replacement for all provider assurance documentation
reason: Artifact supplies relevant AWS compliance documents. A customer workload still needs assessment of its own controls and intended use; provider reports are not blanket application certification.
visual: AWS compliance reports + customer controls/evidence → workload assessment; show shared-responsibility split.

stem: A business deploys an internal assistant through a managed AWS foundation-model service. The project owner wants accountable governance for company data and the customer-facing application. Which TWO responsibilities remain with the customer?
options: Define and enforce appropriate user and workload permissions
Review approved data use and monitor application behavior against business requirements
Physically secure and replace the underlying AWS-managed data-center hardware
Let the model infer authorization from conversational wording instead of explicit policies
Treat every generated confidence statement as an approved compliance assessment
reason: Customers retain responsibilities for identities, data use, configuration and application operation. AWS manages its underlying infrastructure; model confidence does not replace access or governance controls.
visual: Customer governance lifecycle across data approval → access → release review → monitoring; AWS infrastructure responsibilities shown separately.
